titleStmt.title: Towards Free Task Overloading in Passive Replication Based Real-time Multiprocessors

analytic.title: Towards Free Task Overloading in Passive Replication Based Real-time Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In multiprocessor systems, passive replication is a technique that trades processing power for increased reliability. One approach of passive replication, called primary-backup task scheduling, is often used in real-time multiprocessor systems to ensure that deadlines are met in spite of faults. Briefly, it consists in scheduling a secondary task conditionally, in such a way that the secondary task actually gets executed only if the primary task (or the processor executing it) fails to terminate properly. Doing so avoids wasting CPU resources in failure-free case, but primary and secondary tasks must then compete for resources in case of failures. To overcome this, overloading schemes, such as primary-backup overloading, backup-backup overloading and their hybrid, aim at improving schedulability while retaining a certain level of reliability.

Traditionally primary-backup overloading is related to small scale embedded and real-time systems. However, as the fast development of computer systems the implementation of these schemes becomes a difficult mission especially when there are many processors in large scale embedded and real-time systems, multi-core or many-core systems or when the schemes are adopted to realize passive replication in a cluster or a datacenter for soft real-time applications. In this paper, we formalize overloading management towards free overloading, and then some principles are proved to simplify the construction and destruction of overloading in scheduling tasks and tolerating faults.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, it is essential that tasks are completed before their deadlines even in the presence of processor or task failures. In real-time multiprocessor systems, fault-tolerance can be provided by redundantly scheduling copies of tasks on different processors [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Primary-backup scheduling is one instance of fault-tolerant scheduling. In primary-backup task scheduling, two copies of a task, namely primary and backup, are scheduled on two different processors. The backup task is executed if and only if the primary task fails. Hence, primary-backup technique is a kind of passive replication.

To improve the schedulability (i.e., the total number of tasks that can be scheduled), overloading is often adopted. Primary-backup overloading (called PB for short) allows that the primary copy of a task to be scheduled onto a processor *In this paper, Naixue Xiong is the corresponding author. and its running time slot overlaps with the time slot of the backup copy of another task [7]. Backup-backup overloading (BB) only allows that backup copies overlap with each other, but not with primary copies [5], [6], [7]. In [7] it is shown that PB is able to achieve better schedulability than BB, which is in turn weaker than BB in terms of reliability. As a good tradeoff between PB and BB, hybrid overloading is proposed to extend overloading techniques flexibly and freely [8]. It is easy to overload two or three tasks together and the overloading management, constructing overloading and destructing overloading, is also simple such as in [5], [6], [7]. However, to manage overloading becomes formidable and is too complex to implement directly when more tasks are overloaded together. It is necessary to carefully study the overloading management for simplifying programming and implementation in practice. Unfortunately, little research has been focused on this topic in the literature. In this paper, the first contribution is to formalize overloading management for the existing overloading schemes, and then, some principles are discussed and proved. All of these principles can be used to simplify the implementation of overloading techniques in real-time multiprocessor systems, although no specific algorithm or implementation is shown in this paper. The another contribution is to build an analytical basis for further study.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents a brief review of related work and the problems of overloading management. Section III introduces the models and the definitions for formalizing overloading management. The principles of overloading management are introduced and proved in Section IV. How to design the related algorithms based on the free task overloading technique is briefly illustrated in Section V. Finally, we conclude this paper in Section VI.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK AND PROBLEMS
div.p: In primary-backup task scheduling, the backup copies often refer to "ghost" tasks [10]; a backup is scheduled only conditionally and is removed upon the successful completion of its primary [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Overloading schemes schedule multiple tasks in the same time interval to improve system utilization. BB has been proposed in [5] and PB has been shown as an improvement of BB in [7]. In [7], it is shown that BB has an advantage in reliability and PB defeats BB for schedulability. To compromise BB and PB, hybrid overloading has been introduced in [8]. Let pr i denote a primary, bk i denote a backup and P i denote a processor. The three overloading schemes are instanced in Fig. 1.

The existing BB-and PB-overloading limit only two tasks (two backups or a primary and a backup) can be overloaded [5], [6], [4], [7]. BB and PB limit that a small number of tasks are allowed to be overloaded together. These limits come into being because first it is difficult to manage many overloaded tasks and second long chains are unreliable.

For example, in Fig. 1, if the task pr 1 in the BB fails, bk 1 and pr 2 will survive and bk 2 will be deleted to tolerate the fault in pr 1 . After the destruction of the overloading, the remaining tasks cannot tolerate a new fault. If the task pr 1 in the PB fails, bk 1 and bk 2 will survive and pr 2 will be deleted to tolerate the fault in pr 1 . After the destruction of the overloading, the remaining tasks cannot tolerate a new fault. If bk 2 in both the BB and the PB is scheduled to finish very late, the system will be unreliable for a long time.

In order to tolerate more faults the overloading is limited only in a subset of all processors, and then it is possible to tolerate a new fault in the whole system if the new fault does not happen in the subset. This solution is named grouping technique in [6], [7], which can be classified into static grouping and dynamic grouping. The overloading chain is possible to be extended longer, especially for a more robust system or a soft real-time system. In a SMP with many processors or a large multi-core or manycore system, the number of simultaneous processor or core failures may not be very high and then overloading obviously is possible across the system scale but not a small set of processors or cores. In a huge cluster or a datacenter which provides soft real-time application such air ticket booking system, overloading may exist in a set of many computing nodes through dynamic grouping. Neither BB nor PB is flexible enough to allocate tasks freely. Hence, hybrid overloading appears. However it is difficult to schedule tasks to construct overloading or to delete tasks to destruct overloading for either longer BB and PB or hybrid overloading. Whenever to schedule a task or to delete a task, the system has to understand the relation among tasks. Without a good overloading management which includes how to represent overloading, how to efficiently decide task allocation and deletion and how to guarantee the validity of overloading, the programming and implementation of overloading schemes are annoying and complicated.

Overloading management is absent in the literature because tasks are overloaded in a very simple way for the limits shown in the above. In [9], tasks overloaded in the same time interval are looked as a task set and the task sets are managed by the scheduler. Because the scheduling algorithm and the target system in [9] implicitly limit the overloading, the plain implementation is feasible for the simple relation of tasks. In [8], the different overloading schemes appear with different probabilities through an analysis based on stochastic models. In this paper, we do not consider in which conditions the complex overloading can appear, and we only study how to manage overloading. The detailed problem will be addressed later along with system models and definitions.

div.head: III. MODELS AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: The system model considered in this paper is similar to those found in the literature [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. All tasks arrive at a scheduler which schedules them on a firstcome first-served basis. The tasks are then dispatched to other processors, and executed according to their schedule. All processors have identical computing capability and are connected through a network. The scheduler is running in parallel with the processors. Each processor has its own task queue. We assume that the scheduler never fails, either because it runs on a fault-proof processor, or because it has been replicated. The total number of processors is m.

The fault in this paper is defined that a processor fails for some reasons such as hardware or software problems and the tasks in this processor are lost whether the processor is recovered or not. Thus, the faults can be transient or permanent. The fault is assumed to be detected in time by a fault detector.

Tasks are asynchronous and aperiodic, i.e., task arrivals are not known in advance. Each task t i has the following numeric characteristics: ready time (r i ), worst-case computation time (c i ) and deadline (d i ). A task and its copy are identical. The one which will be executed earlier is said to be the primary (pr i ) and the other one is the backup (bk i ). After a primary has finished successfully, its backup is immediately canceled. The outputs of the primary and its backup are always identical. In other words, the tasks are idempotent. Tasks are not parallelizable. A task can be executed only on one single processor exclusively. Tasks are independent. For tasks with precedence constraints, the deadlines of tasks can be modified to make tasks comply with their precedence constraints [6]. Tasks are non-preemptable.

After the allocation of a task is decided, the start time and the finish time of this task are known. Let St(t i ) denote the start time and F t(t i ) denote the end time of task t i . Let P roc(t i ) denote the processor on which task t i is scheduled. Since the two copies, primary and backup, of a task must be scheduled with space and time exclusion, the following rules exist. Rule 1: r i ≤ St(pr i ) < F t(pr i ) < St(bk i ) < F t(bk i ) ≤ d i Rule 2: P roc(pr i ) = P roc(bk i ) Rule 3: If P roc(pr i ) = P roc(pr j ), then [St(pr i ), F t(pr i )] ∩ [St(pr j ), F t(pr j )] = φ The models introduced in the above represent primarybackup task systems in the literature. But they only supports the simple overloading schemes, such as pure PB and BB with a few tasks. In order to represent complex overloading schemes, it is necessary to formalize overloading management with more details.

When the running times of two tasks in a processor are overlapped, the two tasks are said to be overloaded. When any two tasks in a set of tasks in a processor are overloaded, the task set is said to be an overloading task set τ . Hence, in a task set τ , we know
div.formula: ∀t i ∈ τ, ∀t j =i ∈ τ, [St(t i ), F t(t i )] ∩ [St(t j ), F t(t j )] = φ
div.p: Similarly, for a task set τ , the start time and the end time are defined to be
div.formula: St(τ ) = min{St(t i )|∀t i ∈ τ } and F t(τ ) = max{F t(t i )|∀t i ∈ τ }.
div.p: Here, t i can be either primary or backup.

According to the types of tasks in task set τ , we can define the type of task set. A task set τ i only containing primary is defined to be π set, π type or simply τ i = π; a task set τ i only containing backups is defined to be β set, β type or simply τ i = β; a task set τ i containing both primary and backups is defined to be η set, η type or simply τ i = η. There is a special case in terms of the definition of task set: a single task, a primary or a backup, is also a task set.

No matter what kind of overloading, the task sets are connected by their relations through overloading. Hence, the task sets and their relations can be represented as a graph G S (V S , E S ), even under the existing rules. V S is the set of task sets and E S is the set of edges each of which is a relation between task sets. We define the directions of edges to be from a primary to its backup, and then G S is also a directed graph. A single task can be looked as a task set and a single task set is also a single node graph. Thus, |V S | ≥ 1 and |E S | ≥ 0. As tasks arrive and depart, a G S is dynamically changed.With grouping techniques, task overloading can tolerate more than one fault. We only consider one fault during the life time of a G S because we do not deal with grouping technique in this paper. If a G S is a pure primary-backup overloading, the G S is said to be P type or simply
div.formula: G S = G P . If a G S is a pure backup-backup overloading, the G S is said to be B type or G S = G B . If a G S is a hybrid overloading, the G S is said to be H type or G S = G H . Hereinafter,without specific appointment, a G S can be any of G P , G B and G H .
div.p: Overloading management is formalized as to manage a set of G S . If a new task is added into a G S aware of the complex relations among task sets to avoid incorrect overloading, it is necessary to check each task set and the tasks inside the task set and then confirm the task allocation as what has been done in [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. If there are k task sets in a G S , generally without taking an optimized algorithm the time complexity of adding a new task is Θ(k 2 ). Assuming there are g task graphs and each graph has k task sets, the time complexity of adding a new task into the system is Θ(gk 2 ). The same operations should be taken when a fault happens. Moreover, lots of additional information and data should be stored along with the task sets to implement the management of the system. For example, at least the graphs should be memorized to denote the relations among tasks.

div.head: IV. OVERLOADING MANAGEMENT
div.p: The main problem of managing overloaded tasks is that the relation among tasks must be understood by overloading management. Whatever adding a new task or deleting an old task, the operations must be aware of the relation. A complicated overloading management first is difficult to implement and second is fragile. Overloading management is hoped to work without knowing too much about the relations. In other words, we hope to simplify overloading management so that a task can be added only if the rules are met. However, a G S may not tolerate faults if the task sets are not scheduled correctly. If a G S cannot tolerate faults, the G S is invalid and overloading management should know how to avoid this invalidity. There is no definition of validity for overloading in the literature except in [8], in which an invalid overloading is simply defined to be a loop existing in a G S . However, it is also necessary to traverse the G S to guarantee that there is no loop. In this paper, around the validity of overloading, a series of theoretical overloading principles are shown. These principles can be used as extra rules in primary-backup task scheduling to simplify overloading management. Lemma 1. Two task sets, τ i and τ j . ∃pr p ∈ τ i and ∃pr q ∈ τ j , if bk p ∈ τ j and bk q ∈ τ i , then τ i and τ j are interacting task sets. In any G S which is built simply following the rules, there are no interacting task sets.
Proof: Since for any task, the rules must be satisfied, given pr p ∈ τ i , pr q ∈ τ j and bk p ∈ τ j , from Rule 1 we can know
div.formula: St(pr p ) < F t(pr p ) < St(bk p ) < F t(bk p ) St(pr q ) < F t(pr q ) < St(bk q ) < F t(bk q )
div.p: and because bk p ∈ τ j and pr q ∈ τ j ,
div.formula: [St(pr q ), F t(pr q )] ∩ [St(bk p ), F t(bk p )] = φ.
div.p: Therefore, we have St(bk p ) < F t(pr q ) and then F t(pr p ) < St(bk q ).
Consequently,
[St(pr p ), F t(pr p )] ∩ [St(bk q ), F t(bk q )] = φ.
Hence, bk q / ∈ τ . There are no interacting task sets, if the rules are met.

Corollary 1. As two interacting task sets do not exist in any G S , more interacting task sets do not exist in any G S either, such as ∃pr p ∈ τ i , ∃pr q ∈ τ j , ∃pr r ∈ τ k and bk p ∈ τ j , bk q ∈ τ k , bk k ∈ τ i .
Proof: Based on Lemma 1, this is very easy to prove by mathematical induction. Hence, this proof is omitted. Theorem 1. A G S is valid, iff. ∀τ i ∈ V S and ∀τ j =i ∈ V S , P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ).

Proof: First we prove the necessity by contradiction. Assuming ∃τ i ∈ V S and ∃τ j ∈ V S with P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ), when a permanent fault happens in P roc(τ i ), G S will be destructed and in the worst case (the overloading fully collapses) only one task will survive in the remaining task sets. The remaining tasks are obviously not able to tolerate a second fault because each remaining task has no additional copy existing in the system. While P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ), if the fault of τ i is tolerated by destructing G S , the remaining task in τ j has to face the second fault because the fault is a permanent processor failure. Hence, G S is invalid.

Second we prove the sufficiency. Whatever the tasks are overloaded and added into a G S , no problem will happen without any failure only if all rules can be met, because in fact no backups can interfere with primaries as a backup is deleted as soon as its primary finishes. Hence we should care about the destruction of G S in case any failure happens. When to destruct a G S with only a primary and a backup, there is also no problem, since we have proved that there are no interacting task sets in Lemma 1. However, when to destruct a G S with more than 2 task sets, it is possible to fail to destruct a G S into separated tasks in the worst case, as at least two tasks may remain in a task set. Because the task sets in G S are connected, we can always find such a path in G S (V S , E S ), • • • pr i , bk i-1 pr i+1 , bk i pr i+2 , bk i+1 • • •, even if there are other branches to this path and other tasks in each task set. When a failure happens, if there are two fault task sets in the right and the left of pr i+1 , bk i to destruct the path from the two ends, such as both pr i , bk i-1 and pr i+2 , bk i+1 being failed, both pr i+1 and bk i must survive. According to the defined task system, a task must be executed exclusively in one processor. Hence, a path as shown above cannot be destructed from two ends. Because we only consider one fault during the life time of a G S , the only reason to simultaneously lose two task sets is that the two task sets are in the same processor. For any path like the above one in G S , no two task sets can be in the same processor. Hence, if G S is valid, ∀τ i ∈ V S and ∀τ j =i ∈ V S , P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ).

It is desirable that overloading can be achieved with only simple rules and without much knowledge of task relations. Theorem 1 provides a new principle, which can guarantee that the overloading is effective to tolerate a fault if the overloading is constructed by the rules in Section 3 and this principle. Thus, we add a new rule as Rule 4: ∀τ i ∈ V S and ∀τ j =i ∈ V S , P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ).

With the four rules, we do not need to care about what the overloading looks like and any G S which meets the rules is able to tolerate a fault. But, until now we only know that the task sets will be in a fault tolerant graph. However, the destruction still needs to carefully traverse all the overloaded task sets in G S (V S , E S ) to tolerate the fault, because we do not know the structure of a G S which is constructed only through the rules. Hence, it is also still necessary to memory the graphs. In order to simplify the problem, we add a new constraint to task sets.

Although two primaries cannot be overloaded, in a task set there are possible two primaries as shown in Fig. 2. If no more Fig. 2. Two primaries in a task set than one primary is allowed to appear in any task set i.e., |{pr i ∈ τ }| ≤ 1., the graph of task sets will degrade to a tree of task set. In the following, we formally prove the graph is a rooted and directed tree and there are some results helpful to fast decide whether a new task can be added into a task set.
div.formula: Corollary 2. A G S (V S , E S ) is a simple directed graph.
div.p: Proof: It is not necessary to prove that a G S (V S , E S ) is a directed graph. We only prove G S (V S , E S ) is simple. From Lemma 1, Corollary 1 and Theorem 1, we know that there is no loop in any G S (V S , E S ). Because there is at most one primary in a task set and any edge of G S (V S , E S ) must originate from a primary, the out-degree of any π ∈ V S or η ∈ V S is 1, the in-degree of π ∈ V S is 0, the out-degree of any β ∈ V S is 0 and the in-degrees of η and β are greater than or equal to 1, i.e., deg
Obviously, there is no two vertices connected by multiple edges in G S (V S , E S ). Hence, an G S (V S , E S ) is a simple directed graph.
div.formula: Corollary 3. If a G S is valid, then |V S | ≤ m.
div.p: Proof: This is easy to know from Theorem 1. Theorem 1 requires ∀τ i ∈ V S and ∀τ j =i ∈ V S , P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ). The number of processors is m. If |V S | > m at least two tasks are in the same processor, i.e, ∃τ i ∈ V S , ∃τ j =i ∈ V S and P roc(τ i ) = P roc(τ j ). Thus, such an G S is invalid. Hence, we have |V S | ≤ m.

Proof: We first prove there is a task set only containing backups, ∃β ∈ V S , and then prove there is only one such task set, i.e., |{β ∈ V S }| = 1. When only one task is in a G S , i.e., two task sets, a π and a β, obviously there is only one β. Adding the second task into the G S , whether choosing PB or BB, there is still only one β, because there are no interacting task sets according to Lemma 1 and Corollary 1. To add the third task sets, the result is the same that only one β is in the G S . Assuming that n tasks have been in the G S and that there is only one β in the G S , let us consider adding the n + 1 th task. If pr i+1 is added to the β because a primary cannot be overloaded into a π or a η, then bk i+1 becomes the only β, since G S is simple directed graph according to Corollary 2. If bk i+1 is overloaded into the β, there is still only one β. By mathematical induction, we know there is only one β. This Lemma can also be proved by the following Lemmas. Here we only show the proof by mathematical induction. Theorem 2. A G S is a rooted and directed tree. The root is a β. All leaves are π. All internal vertices are η, if the internal vertices exist.

Proof: A G S is a simple directed graph and all vertices are connected. A simple graph is naturally a tree. Hence in order to prove this theorem, it is only necessary to prove that all vertices are led by the edges to the root, which is a β. From Lemma 2, we know in G S there is only one β. From Corollary 2, we know deg

div.p: Thus, in a G S , a β is the only vertex without ancestor. Hence, a β is the root of a G S . Given any task set τ other than the β in the G S , τ can only be π or η, any one of which will leave a backup bk in either a η or the β. If bk ∈ β, then τ is led to the root. If bk ∈ η, then the η will repeatedly leave another bk in either a η or the β. This process will repeat. Because, there is no loop in G S and |V S | is finite. The process can only end at the β. Since any task set is connected to the root through the directed edges, a G S is a rooted and directed tree. Because only one primary can be in a task set, a π only contains a primary. Now that deg -(π) = 0 and deg + (π) = 1, a π is a leaf. A η must contain at least a primary and a backup. As a result, η must have parent and child in the tree. Thus, only π can be leaf and only η can be internal vertices. The proof is complete.
Note that the direction of path in a rooted tree is usually from the root to the leaves [11]. The natural direction of path in a G S is from the leaf to the root. But this does not hamper the proofs.

1) For the only β in G S , |β| is the maximum when all the primaries in G S have their backups in β. Therefore, |β| ≤ m -1. 2) For any η, if it exists in G S , |η| is the maximum when all the primaries except itself have their backups in η.

Corollary 3 and 4 show the maximal sizes of G S and τ . The sizes can be used to faster decide task allocations. Overloading management does not need to check the task set with the maximal task sizes or the G S which reaches the maximal capacity. It is easy to document the processors a G S has visited, for example binary coding the processors. Hence, it is easy to construct a G S simply by the rules.

As for what G S looks like, Theorem 2 shows the answer that finally the G S must be a rooted and directed tree. This is a strong principle by which it is easy to destruct a G S . For example, overloading management can handle parents and children recursively in different policies to destruct G S , starting from the failed task set. Moreover, a G S does not need to be fully destructed if the tree can be decomposed into parts which all only need to correctly handle the vertices connect themselves. As tasks can be scheduled freely only if the rules and principles are committed, we can simply name a new overloading technique to be free overloading. Hence, effective and efficient algorithms without memorizing the structure of the tree can be designed in terms of the previous principles, but in this paper, we do not show any detailed algorithm. We show an example in Fig. 3. To overloaded tasks like those in Fig. 3, it is only necessary to simply obey the rules and finally the task sets will become a tree as in Fig. 3, and the more important is that we do not need to memorize the structure of the tree when adding a new task or destructing the overloading for fault tolerance.

The tree is naturally created by the rules and shows the logical relation among tasks. If we add more constraints to task sets, the task sets can also be managed as a list of task sets. If the tasks in a task set are overloaded tightly enough so that

div.formula: Lemma 3. In a G S , if St(τ k ) = min{St(τ i )|τ i ∈ V S }, then τ k = π or τ k = η. τ k starts from a primary. If τ k is tight, only τ k = π.
div.p: Proof: This lemma is proved by contradiction. If τ k = β, ∃bk j ∈ τ k and St(τ k ) = St(bk j ). Since all rules must be met, ∃pr j ∈ G S and F t(pr j ) < St(bk j ). No matter how short the running time of pr j is, we know St(pr j ) < F t(pr j ). Thus, we have St(pr j ) < St(τ k ). This contradicts St(τ k ) = min{St(τ i )|τ i ∈ V S }. Thus, τ k = β and ∃pr ∈ τ k . Since ∀bk j ∈ τ k , St(τ k ) = St(bk j ), there must be St(τ k ) = St(pr ), i.e., τ k starts from a primary. If ∃bk j ∈ τ k and τ k is tight, according to the definition of task set, we know

div.p: Proof: This lemma is also proved by contradiction. If ∃pr j ∈ τ k and F t(τ k ) = F t(pr j ), then ∃bk j ∈ G S and F t(τ k ) = F t(pr j ) < St(bk j ) from the rules and the definition of task set. This contradicts F t(τ k ) = max{F t(τ i )|τ i ∈ S}. Thus, τ k = π because in a π there is only a primary. If τ k = η, i.e., ∃pr j ∈ τ k , then F t(τ k ) = F t(pr j ). In other words, τ k only ends at a backup. If ∃pr j ∈ τ k and τ k is tight, according to the definition of task set, we know
div.formula: St(τ k ) ≤ St(pr i ) < F t(pr i ) < St(bk i ) < F t(bk i ) ≤ F t(τ k ) and then F t(τ k ) -St(τ k ) ≥ 2M in(c i ).
div.p: From the definition of tight task set, we know
div.formula: F t(τ k ) -St(τ k ) ≥ c j + , < c i .
div.p: As a result, for a tight task set,
div.formula: 2M in(c i ) > F t(τ k ) -St(τ k ) ≥ M in(c i ) + .
div.p: Obviously, there is a contradiction. Hence, if τ k is tight, no primary can be in τ k and then τ k = β. In a G B only π sets and one β exist. Because any primary has a backup behind it, the β in a G B is the latest task set. Thus, if
div.formula: G S = G B , τ k = β.
div.p: Intuitionally the first task set and the last task set in a G S should be a π and a β respectively. Logically, according to Theorem 2, the leaves must be earlier than the internal vertices and the root. However, due to the diversity of task running time, the first task set and the last task set might be η. The fact is shown in Fig. 4. Proof: As proved in Theorem 2, a G S is a rooted and directed tree only if the tasks are overloaded into G S by meeting the rules. Naturally, a G B can be managed as a tree, since we know it is only necessary to add a new primary as a leaf and to overload its backup into the root of the tree to maintain G S = G B . As we know the target of overloading management is to construct and destruct any G S efficiently and effectively. Hence, we only need to show that it is feasible to construct G S = G B and destruct G S if the task sets are sorted by end time in a list. According to Lemma 4, if G S = G B and F t(τ k ) = max{F t(τ i )|τ i ∈ S}, we always have τ k = β. Therefore, the list of task sets sorted by end time must end at a β, which is unique in terms of Lemma 2. Because of G S = G B , there is no η in G S . Thus, in the task set list, the last task set is a β and the task sets in front of the β are π. When adding a new task into this G B , it only need to insert a π containing the primary before the β and insert the backup into the β on condition that all rules and the previous results are satisfied. Since the relation of task sets can be easily understood through the structure of the task set list, the destruction is also easily performed. It is not necessary to explain the destruction in details. Thus, a list of task sets sorted by end time can be used to manage a G B . Corollary 6. Only if a G P is tight, the G P can be managed to be a timely sorted task set list.

Proof: Obviously, a G P can be managed as a logical list, a special case of the rooted tree proved in Theorem 2. This logical list can be denoted as π, η 1 , η 2 , • • •, β. From the proof of Corollary 5, we can know G P can be managed as a timely sorted list if the relation of task sets can be easily understood through the structure of the task set list. If G P is not tight, the first task is a π or a η in terms of Lemma 3 and the last task is a β or a η in a timely sorted task set list. Thus, it is impossible to confirm the relation among tasks because the first task set in the logical list should be a π and the last task set should be a β. If G P is tight, according to Lemma 3 and Lemma 4, the head and the tail of the timely sorted list are equivalent to the logical list. If we delete the head and the tail from the timely sorted list, the remaining list still meet Lemma 3 and Lemma 4 and the head and the tail in the remaining list are also equivalent to those in the logical list in which the head and the tail are also deleted. In this way, recursively we can know each task set in the timely sorted list is equivalent to that in the logical list for the relation of task sets. Hence, the proof is complete.

A list is just a special case of a tree. Although PB and BB can be managed as lists of task sets, they can also be managed as trees of task sets. As shown in Theorem 2, Lemma 3 and Lemma 4, free overloading cannot be represented by either logically sorted task set list or timely sorted task set list. However, in fact, to manage as list is not much simpler than to manage as tree, because free overloading does not need to keep the overloading types in mind.

div.head: V. DESIGNING ALGORITHMS
div.p: The most benefit of adopting free task overloading in passive replication fault tolerant multiprocessors is that there is no need to memorize the relation among the overloaded tasks whenever the overloading is constructed and destructed. In this way, the complexity of the related algorithms and the implementation of systems can be reduced. It is very simple to verify the previously existing rules since a scheduling algorithm only needs to compute the known numeric attributes of tasks instantly. Each G S can be attached a binary code to represent the processors which have been visited. Thus, to verify Rule 4, only simple operations of "AND" or "OR" should be performed on the binary codes. Hence, a scheduling algorithm only needs to cost additional O(4) time at most in verifying all the rules in allocating each task. Each task schedule contains several G S , and in the above we have proved that each G S must be valid to tolerate faults. It is not necessary to redesign a fault tolerant task scheduling algorithm for real-time multiprocessors. Any scheduling algorithm which schedules tasks one by one can be modified to meet the rules and then it is fault tolerant. Because of the space limit of the paper, we do not show any instance of a fault tolerant scheduling algorithm based on the free overloading technique. Instead, we focus on the algorithms which tolerate faults.

Without the information of the relation among tasks, it seems difficult to destruct the overloading to tolerate faults like those done in Fig. 1. However, we have proved the relation can be represented by a rooted and directed tree, such as that in Fig. 3. For each type of task sets, the destructing methods are fixed. For example, if a task set is destructed from a backup due to a chain reaction from another task set, the backup must be reversed as its primary version and all the other tasks in this task set should be deleted. The loss of a primary must cause reversing a backup in another task set. Hence, we can design a recursive algorithm to handle the faults. We show an example as follows. In the example, we assume that in each task set the information of neighbor task set is available. Thus, in a G S , for each task t i of a task set τ , i.e., τ.t i , τ.neighbor i denotes the neighbor task set linked to t i which is a primary or a backup. The example includes two algorithms. The first algorithm deals with the failed task sets and the second one handles the chain reaction recursively. Here, revs(taskset, task) is a method which reverses a task to its opposite version. Without further proof, we can know the example costs at most O(n) time to destruct a G S if there are n task sets because the example deals with each task set at most once.

Although this paper is limited to discuss the rules and the conditions which make rooted and directed trees, the algorithms shown above are also feasible when a G S is a simple directed graph by loosing the overloading conditions. Nonetheless, the scheduling algorithms for the graphs have to be more complicated than the ones for the trees.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we formalize primary-backup task overloading management by defining different types of task set, different types of graphs of task sets and the related terms and concepts. Overloading management is defined to manage the graphs with the rules and principles, some from the literature and the others proved in this paper. Through proving the principles, it is shown that overloading management only need to commit the rules and the principles in constructing an overloading and not necessary to know what the overloading will be. It is proved finally the overloading becomes a rooted and directed tree if all rules and principles are committed. Thus, it is not difficult to design effective and efficient algorithms to destruct or recompose the overloading. A few of numeric results are also provided to enhance the efficiency of overloading management. We also show that a PB or a BB can be managed as a list of timely sorted task sets under some conditions. Compared to the existing overloading schemes, the overloading management in this paper aims at freely overloading and in this way the overloading management is simplified and can be easily programmed and implemented.

As we know from this paper, by enhancing the constraints on task sets, the overloaded tasks can be managed as graphs, trees or lists. For trees and lists, it is not necessary to memorize the structure of the overloading. The constructing and destructing of the overloading can be performed by simply following the rules and recursive algorithms. Hence, the overloading management does not need to traverse all task sets. Thus, we name this kind of overloading to be free overloading. However, more constraints on task sets will limit the flexibility of the overloading and then the schedulability has to be trade for the reliability. According to the results in this paper, it is a good tradeoff by limiting only one primary in a task set to manage the tasks as a rooted and directed tree.

Based on the results in this paper, some efficient algorithms for overloading management could be designed. In the future there are still some issues worthy of careful study. For example, despite that two primaries cannot be overloaded, two primaries may be allowed to overlap the same backups. In this case, the overloaded tasks have to be managed as graphs but not trees or can be continually granted by defining coupled trees. Obviously, the preconditions of overloading management can be modified only if the basic rules are kept, and then some new results may emerge and some old ones may collapse. Nonetheless, the work in this paper provide an analysis basis for future exploiting.
